paper_title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large Language Model inference over long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of attending to a growing Key-Value (KV) cache. Sparse attention reduces this cost by accessing only a fraction of the cache, but existing methods face a trade-off between deterministic retrieval, which captures high-scoring tokens but discards residual attention mass, and sampling, which improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combine top-$k$ retrieval with uniform sampling, yet still exhibit a substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. We introduce \emph{Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA)}, a unified framework combining deterministic retrieval with score-guided sampling. SSA deterministically attends to high-scoring tokens while sampling the residual using proxy attention scores and correcting for their inclusion probabilities, thereby recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set. SSA encompasses top-$k$, top-$p$, and hybrid top-$k$+sampling as special cases. Across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME, and five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, SSA consistently improves over the baselines at matched sparsity. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B, SSA improves accuracy over the strongest practical baseline from 81.8\% to 84.2\% at 32K and from 63.8\% to 69.3\% at 128K under $50\times$ attention sparsity, recovering 94\% and 85\% of dense-attention performance, respectively. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA achieves up to $2.96\times$ decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context, demonstrating that its accuracy gains translate into practical long-context inference acceleration. We open-source our code at https://github.com/skylight-org/SSA-Paper-Code.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding into long-context workloads, spanning large document collections [23], image analysis [10, 31], software engineering [15, 5], databases [48], video processing [33], and long-horizon agents that continuously accumulate observations, tool outputs, and interaction histories [3, 4]. As context lengths approach millions of tokens, efficient inference becomes increasingly challenging. During autoregressive decoding, each newly generated token attends to an ever-growing key-value (KV) cache, requiring keys and values to be repeatedly transferred from GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) onto on-chip SRAM for attention computation [35, 20]. At long contexts, this makes decoding increasingly memory-bandwidth bound: the attention cost per decoding Equal contribution. Department of Computer Science, Rice University, TX, USA. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by attending to only small fraction of the KV cache [39, 27, 46], reducing both memory traffic and attention latency. However, realizing these gains in practice requires sparse attention to satisfy two competing objectives: faithfully approximate dense attention at aggressive sparsity while remaining efficient enough to translate sparsity into end-to-end inference speedups [29, 25]. Existing sparse-attention methods can be broadly categorized by how they allocate limited attention budget. First, approximate retrieval methods use proxy attention scores to deterministically select high-scoring tokens, typically through top-k retrieval. Representative methods include PQCache [46], and Quest [39], with recent approaches such as Tactic [50] extending this paradigm to top-p selection. While effective when attention is highly concentrated, deterministic retrieval can miss substantial attention mass when the distribution is diffuse or long-tailed [6, 9]. Second, sampling-based methods such as MagicPig [6] use importance sampling to approximate dense attention, providing broader coverage but introducing sampling variance that can lead to larger gap from dense attention at limited budgets (see Table 5 in Appendix). Finally, hybrid methods such as vAttention [9] combine deterministic top-k retrieval with uniform sampling [42], preserving high-confidence tokens while extending coverage beyond the top-k set. Although this combination improves the trade-off between exploitation and coverage, substantial gap to dense attention remains at aggressive sparsity (see Table 5 in Appendix). See Section 2 for more details. These observations motivate fundamental question: Can we design more effective sampling strategy that substantially narrows the sparse-to-dense accuracy gap? Our preliminary studies reveal key limitation of uniform sampling: while it provides coverage beyond the deterministic top-k set, it ignores the highly non-uniform distribution of residual attention mass1. As shown in fig. 1, score-guided importance sampling (the principle that SSA uses) consistently achieves lower relative L2 error than uniform sampling. Motivated by this observation, we introduce Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA), unified framework that combines deterministic retrieval of high-confidence heavy hitters with score-guided stochastic exploration of the remaining context. Rather than treating all residual tokens equally, SSA uses proxy attention scores to preferentially explore promising regions while preserving stochastic coverage of the long tail. This enables the sparse attention budget to better capture the attention mass that would otherwise be lost under aggressive sparsity. Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, Ministral-3-3B-Instruct-2517, and Ministral-3-8B-Instruct-2517 [26], and across RULER [16], LongBench [2], LOFT [22], and AIME [28]. Across these evaluations, SSA consistently improves over deterministic, sampling-based, and hybrid sparse-attention baselines, substantially narrowing the gap to dense attention at extreme sparsity. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: I. Unified Attention Paradigm: We introduce unified sparse-attention framework that partitions tokens into deterministic and stochastic strata using generic proxy score. By varying how tokens are retained or sampled, the framework recovers top-k, top-p, and hybrid top-k+sampling as special cases of importance-sampling-inspired sparse attention. II. Theoretical Guarantees: We provide rigorous bounds for our proposed algorithm, characterizing how closely it approximates dense attention under limited attention budget. III. Efficient Kernel Support: We develop efficient CUDA/Triton kernels that realize the computational benefits of our approach in practice, delivering end-to-end decoding speedups over dense attention.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: In the context of SSA, the extensive prior work can be organized into three broad and comprehensive research directions: Head-level compression and KV eviction: One line of work reduces KV-cache overhead by sharing or compressing KV heads. Multi-Query Attention (MQA) [37] shares single KV head across all query heads, while Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) [1] and Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) [7] provide more flexible compression to balance efficiency and model quality. complementary line of work dynamically evicts less important KV entries during inference. Methods such as SnapKV [24], DynamicKV [49], KVZip [19], KeyDiff [30], CurDKV [34], and CapKV [44] use different importance signals and eviction policies to reduce cache size and subsequent attention computation. These approaches are complementary to sparse attention: KV compression reduces the tokens or representations retained across decoding steps, whereas sparse attention dynamically selects which retained tokens to access for each query. The two can therefore be composed to further reduce memory and decoding costs. 3 Approximate top-k/top-p methods: substantial body of sparse-attention work focuses on finding the tokens with the largest attention scores. Methods such as Quest [39], PQCache [46], SqueezedAttention [14], Adamas [43], SOCKET [18], Sketch-and-Walk [21], RetrievalAttention [27], Loki [38], HashAttention [8], and Double Sparsity [45] employ different proxy scores or retrieval mechanisms to approximate the top-k tokens under dense attention. These methods are effective at recovering high-attention heavy hitters, but fixed top-k selection discards all tokens outside the retrieval set. Consequently, when non-negligible attention mass is distributed across the residual tail, or when approximation error causes relevant tokens to fall just below the top-k boundary, this discarded mass can create substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. Tactic [50] extends this retrieval paradigm from top-k to top-p selection by modeling the decay of attention scores with power-law distribution and estimating the number of highest-scoring tokens required to satisfy target attentionmass threshold. Sampling-based and Hybrid methods: MagicPig [6] addresses the limitations of deterministic top-k attention by using LSH [17] to approximately sample tokens and importance correction to estimate dense attention. vAttention [9] combines deterministic and stochastic selection through verified hybrid estimator that retains top-k tokens while uniformly sampling from the residual KV cache. KNN-Attention [13] also explores top-k plus sampling via lazy Gumbel sampling, but primarily targets training rather than inference acceleration for existing models. Unlike uniform hybrid sampling, which treats all residual tokens equally, SSA uses approximate attention scores to guide stochastic selection toward tokens more likely to carry residual attention mass (see fig. 1).

sections.content: Importance sampling [41] is Monte Carlo technique for estimating quantity using samples drawn from proposal distribution. Given target distribution p(x) and function (x), consider the expectation µ = Exp[f (x)] = p(x)f (x). Instead of sampling directly from p(x), importance sampling draws samples x1, . . . , xm q(x) from proposal distribution q(x) and rewrites the expectation as µ = Exq . This yields the Monte Carlo estimator p(x) q(x) (x) ˆµ = 1 X j=1 p(xj) q(xj) (xj). The ratio p(x)/q(x) is the importance weight, which corrects for sampling from rather than p. When places greater probability on samples with large contributions to the expectation, importance sampling can achieve lower variance than uniform sampling with the same sample budget. 4 Introducing Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA) As already mentioned, deterministic top-k attention [11, 47] can omit meaningful attention mass outside the selected set. Uniform sampling on residual tokens provides broader coverage, but does not use information about which remaining tokens are more likely to matter. We introduce Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA), unified framework that retains tokens with high proxy scores and samples the residual tokens according to those scores. SSA divides fixed attention budget between two well-known complementary objectives: exploitation, by deterministically retaining high-confidence heavy hitters, and exploration, by sampling the residual context according to proxy attention scores. This score-aware stratification preserves heavy hitters while providing meaningful stochastic coverage toward more promising residual tokens. sections.title: 4.3 Kernel Design
sections.content: At long contexts, decode attention is memory-bandwidth bound because each step reads the entire KV cache from HBM [35, 20]. SSA reduces this memory traffic by selecting sparse subset of tokens before loading their KV states. While Algorithm 1 determines the division between the heavy and residual strata adaptively, our optimized GPU implementation uses fixed heavy fraction. Developing an equally efficient implementation of the adaptive algorithm remains future work. As shown 7 in Table 4, the practical fixed-budget variant closely matches the performance of the theoretical formulation. The residual proposal, inclusion-probability correction, and resulting attention estimator remain unchanged. Our SSA decode step consists of four stages, where only the first three scan the full context using few bytes per token. Proxy scoring: Each key is represented by 16-byte PQ code (16 subspaces, 256 centroids) [46], compared to 1 KiB for its fp16 key-value pair at head dimension 256. For each query, lookup table computes the proxy score si for every token. Scores are scaled and masked for sink and local tokens within the same kernel, avoiding an additional pass. Heavy-set selection: We select using radix top-k [36], which returns an unsorted index set since the estimator in eq. 2 is invariant to the ordering of selected tokens. Residual sampling: Direct sampling from the full residual distribution becomes expensive at long context lengths, as constructing and sampling from the distribution requires processing probabilities across the entire residual KV cache. To reduce this overhead, we use hierarchical sampler that progressively narrows the search space. Each draw first selects 1024-token chunk, then 32-token sub-tile, and finally scans at most 32 tokens to select key. We remove duplicate samples with per-row hash table and reweight each unique sample by 1/πi. In practice, we clamp πi at 104 to avoid excessively large weights, at the cost of introducing small bias. Finally, we use counter-based random number generator to obtain fresh samples across replays while retaining compatibility with CUDA graph capture. Sparse decode: The final stage gathers the keys and values in from the paged KV cache and evaluates eq. 2 using an online softmax. To exploit more parallelism, we divide each query head across multiple thread blocks and combine their partial softmax results using numerically stable log-sum-exp reduction. At 1M context and batch size 1, using 64 splits is 1.58-1.71 faster than using 32 splits across sparsity levels. Increasing the number of splits to 128 or 256, however, reduces performance because the additional parallelism no longer offsets the increased launch and merge overhead.

sections.title: 5.3 Decode Efficiency
sections.content: Sparse attention accelerates decoding only when its selection overhead is smaller than the memory traffic it saves. We evaluate this trade-off for SSA across context lengths and batch sizes, and separately measure the sampling overhead absent in top-k methods. Efficiency analysis: SSA becomes increasingly advantageous as context length and batch size grow. At batch size 1, SSA is slower than FlashInfer at 128K, achieving approximately 0.60-0.74 its speed. As context length increases, this overhead is increasingly amortized, and SSA reaches 1.79, 1.39, and 1.07 speedups at 1M for 50, 20, and 10 sparsity, respectively (see fig. 3a). The gains 10 further increase with batch size, reaching 2.96 at batch 16 for 50 sparsity (see fig. 3b); our kernel optimizations are particularly important at batch 1, improving SSA by 2.95-3.80 over the reference implementation  (Table 2)  . Finally, although residual sampling introduces overhead absent from top-k methods, our two-level sampler reduces this cost by 1.21-3.16 over chunk-only routing as the number of draws increases (see fig. 3c), keeping sampling latency at 0.30-1.18 ms at 1M context and = 0.4 across the evaluated sparsity levels. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA), unified framework encompassing top-k, pure sampling, and hybrid sparse attention while substantially outperforming existing methods and reducing the accuracy gap to dense attention. SSA is compatible with any approximate top-k method that provides proxy scores, allowing it to directly benefit from advances in approximate retrieval. An important direction for future work is to make SSA verifiable by incorporating user-controlled guarantees on approximation quality.
